orientation: AI product engineering starts with a useful decision. A baseline is the simple existing approach that a new system must improve.
idea: Choose the decision and cost of being wrong before choosing the model.
story: Meera handles equipment-rental messages. Her manager asks for an AI assistant, but the immediate problem is smaller: urgent breakdown reports wait behind routine return questions. The user job is to get each ticket to the right queue quickly.

A keyword rule looks for “broken”. It is cheap and understandable, but “the drill stopped working” slips through. A model may help with phrasing; that still does not prove it reduces the expensive misses. First compare both on the same labelled tickets.
example: On a fictional batch of 20 tickets, a rule gets 18 routes right but misses 2 urgent cases. A model gets 19 right and misses 1 urgent case. That is a useful lead, not proof of readiness: inspect which case failed and test more representative messages.
trap: A fluent reply is not evidence of correct routing. Judge the action the support desk needs, including the mistakes it cannot afford.

lab.question: Which approach best fits a desk that cannot afford missed breakdown reports?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: these are invented routing outcomes for the same 20 tickets, not a running rule engine or model benchmark.

scenarios.label: 1 · Keyword rule
scenarios.result: The rule misses two urgent tickets.
scenarios.why: Overall accuracy hides which errors hurt the desk; review the two missed breakdowns.

scenarios.label: 2 · Mock model
scenarios.result: The mock model improves this batch but still misses one urgent case.
scenarios.why: One additional correct route is evidence about these fixtures only; deployment needs a defined acceptance rule.

scenarios.label: 3 · Route all urgent
scenarios.result: No urgent case is missed, but the urgent queue is flooded.
scenarios.why: A one-sided metric can reward a useless system. Track false alarms and handling capacity alongside missed urgent cases.

mechanism: Write one sentence naming the person, decision and benefit: “Help a support agent route urgent breakdowns promptly.” This keeps the evaluation tied to a real workflow.
Compare a manual or rules baseline and the candidate on the same inputs. Record costly error types separately; a single average can hide an unacceptable tradeoff.
Choose an acceptance boundary before inspecting results. If evidence is too limited, retain human triage and collect more labelled cases instead of treating a demo as a release decision.

transfer.question: An assistant writes beautiful refund replies but still sends tickets to the wrong team. Has it solved this lesson’s user job?
transfer.answer: No. Writing quality is a different outcome from correct routing. Measure routing and its consequences, or explicitly redefine the job.

transfer.question: The model wins on all 20 fixtures. Does that prove it will win next month?
transfer.answer: No. The fixtures may omit new wording, languages or rare urgent events. They support a bounded observation, not a guarantee.

checks.question: What should be written first?
options: The user decision and success measure
A prompt for every possible ticket
checks.explanation: The decision determines what to measure and whether a model is needed.

checks.question: Why is 95% correct insufficient by itself?
options: The remaining errors may be disproportionately costly
checks.explanation: The kind and consequence of the errors matter, as well as their count.

checks.question: What makes a fair baseline comparison?
options: Use easier tickets for the model
Use the same representative cases and decision criteria
checks.explanation: Changing the cases or criteria confounds the comparison.

topics.title: user jobs
topics.explanation: A user job describes progress someone needs to make, not a feature name. “Route a broken drill report quickly” is more testable than “add AI to support”.

topics.title: failure costs
topics.explanation: Different mistakes consume different resources or cause different harm. A routine ticket in the urgent queue costs attention; an urgent ticket in the routine queue delays help, so count both separately.

topics.title: rules versus ML versus generation
topics.explanation: Rules encode explicit conditions, ML learns patterns, and generation produces content. A fixed return-date calculation may need only rules, while varied wording may justify a classifier; generating a paragraph does not automatically improve either decision.

topics.title: baseline
topics.explanation: A baseline is a simple comparison point with measured behaviour. Keep its inputs and scoring aligned with the candidate, and include the current human workflow where relevant.

orientation: A quality metric scores system behaviour. A business metric measures whether the workflow helps, while unit economics asks what one useful outcome costs.
idea: Count the full cost per successful outcome, including human review and failures.
story: Meera’s rental desk receives a proposal: an assistant that costs only ₹2 per ticket. The quote sounds attractive, until she learns that some replies need a staff review and some still fail to resolve the request.

She writes down the denominator: successfully resolved cases. Paying less for each attempted answer can still cost more for each resolution. Now she can compare alternatives using the same fictional batch and a clearly stated success definition.
example: For 100 attempts, model calls cost 100 × ₹2 = ₹200. Reviewing 20 replies costs 20 × ₹15 = ₹300. Total cost is ₹500. If 80 cases are resolved, cost per resolution is ₹500 ÷ 80 = ₹6.25. Unresolved cases still contributed to the bill.
trap: Do not divide only by generated replies and call it cost per resolution. An attempted response, a reviewed response and a resolved customer problem are different events.

lab.question: How does review burden change cost per resolved rental-support case?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: all prices and resolution counts are invented. This is accounting over fixed scenarios, not a pricing quote or a live forecast.

scenarios.label: 1 · Light review
scenarios.result: Total cost is ₹500 for 80 resolutions.
scenarios.why: The numerator includes costs of unresolved attempts too. These figures exclude fixed engineering and support costs.

scenarios.label: 2 · Heavy review
scenarios.result: The same 80 resolutions now cost ₹800.
scenarios.why: Review doubled, even though resolution count did not improve. Lower model-call prices alone would miss this cost driver.

scenarios.label: 3 · Fewer resolutions
scenarios.result: The same ₹500 spend now costs ₹10 per resolution.
scenarios.why: The denominator fell. Measuring only spend per attempted ticket would hide the deterioration.

mechanism: Define “resolved” before counting. For this toy desk, a staff-labelled case is resolved only if the reply correctly settles the customer’s issue; sending text is not enough.
List variable costs over the same period: model calls, review and rework. Add fixed development and operating costs for a full decision, with an explicit allocation assumption.
Set both quality and operational acceptance criteria. A cheaper workflow that mishandles urgent breakdowns can fail the release gate even when its average cost looks good.

transfer.question: A new model halves call cost to ₹100, but review rises to ₹600 and only 50 cases resolve. Is it cheaper than the baseline scenario?
transfer.answer: No. Its stated cost is ₹700 / 50 = ₹14 per resolution, versus ₹6.25. Other uncounted costs could change both totals further.

transfer.question: Does the cheapest scenario necessarily deserve release?
transfer.answer: No. It must also meet quality, capacity and user-outcome criteria. The fixed examples do not measure those criteria for a real service.

checks.question: Which denominator matches cost per resolution?
checks.explanation: Use the outcome named by the metric; unsuccessful attempts still cost money.

checks.question: What happened between light and heavy review?
options: Review cost rose without more resolutions
checks.explanation: Both have 100 calls and 80 resolutions, but review costs rise from ₹300 to ₹600.

checks.question: Which statement is an acceptance criterion?
options: At least 90 of 100 preselected routine cases must resolve correctly
checks.explanation: It names observable behaviour and a threshold. The threshold remains a fictional example, not a universal target.

topics.title: acceptance criteria
topics.explanation: Acceptance criteria specify observable conditions for deciding whether a change is acceptable. “No unsupported promises in the test fixtures” is inspectable; “the bot feels smart” is not.

topics.title: quality metrics
topics.explanation: Quality metrics describe output behaviour, such as correct routing or supported answers. Always state the sample and denominator; a score on routine cases says little about rare urgent reports.

topics.title: business metrics
topics.explanation: Business metrics track outcomes such as resolution time or repeat contacts. They can move differently from answer accuracy because review effort and workflow friction also affect users.

topics.title: unit economics
topics.explanation: Unit economics assigns costs and value to one meaningful unit. Include review and unsuccessful attempts in the numerator, and distinguish variable operating cost from total cost including development.

orientation: Human control means giving people useful ways to clarify, correct or take over. Abstaining means declining to make an unsupported claim; escalation hands the case to someone able to act.
idea: Match the assistant’s action to the evidence and make recovery easy.
story: A customer asks Meera’s rental assistant when a replacement drill will arrive. The order has two addresses and no confirmed dispatch scan. “Tomorrow” would sound helpful, but the assistant does not yet have the facts to promise it.

The useful next action is to ask which address applies. If the carrier records later conflict, the assistant should explain the uncertainty and pass the case to dispatch, carrying the order context so the customer need not repeat everything.
example: One order has a confirmed carrier date, one lacks a delivery address, and one has conflicting tracking records. The appropriate paths are answer with its source, ask a focused question, and hold the promise while escalating. The same friendly tone can accompany all three paths.
trap: A confident voice or a self-reported “95% sure” is not verified evidence. Show what supports the answer and give the customer a practical correction path.

lab.question: What should the assistant do before promising a replacement delivery date?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: the evidence and chosen policy paths are authored examples, not a live assistant or a calibrated uncertainty model.

scenarios.label: 1 · Verified date
scenarios.result: Answer: “The carrier currently lists 14 Oct.”
scenarios.why: A sourced current estimate can be useful without becoming a guarantee. Keep the correction and contact paths available.

scenarios.label: 2 · Missing address
scenarios.result: Ask which saved address should receive the replacement.
scenarios.why: The customer can supply the missing fact. Asking is more useful than guessing or escalating every incomplete request.

scenarios.label: 3 · Conflicting dates
scenarios.result: Explain the conflict and send the case to dispatch.
scenarios.why: Both records exist, but their disagreement is unresolved. More records do not automatically mean stronger evidence.

mechanism: Start by separating missing information from conflicting information. A customer can clarify an address, while dispatch may need to investigate inconsistent carrier records.
Make the next action specific: answer the supported part, ask one useful question, abstain from the unsupported promise, or escalate with the relevant context. These actions can be combined.
Correction should change the workflow, not merely trigger an apology. After the customer fixes an address, confirm what changed and recheck the delivery estimate before sending a new promise.

transfer.question: The customer corrects “Tuesday” to “Thursday”, but the system still schedules Tuesday. Has it supported correction?
transfer.answer: No. The visible acknowledgement did not update the consequential state. Confirm the corrected value and verify the schedule before proceeding.

transfer.question: Should every uncertain request immediately go to a human?
transfer.answer: No. A focused clarification can resolve some gaps. Escalate when policy, authority or unresolved evidence requires it, and make that boundary explicit.

checks.question: Two records disagree about a delivery date. What is justified?
checks.explanation: Conflicting evidence needs reconciliation, not a confident guess.

checks.question: What makes a correction useful?
options: The relevant state and next action reflect it
checks.explanation: A correction must affect the outcome that matters to the customer.

checks.question: Which uncertainty can the customer often resolve directly?
options: Whether a hidden provider outage occurred
checks.explanation: Ask the person who can actually supply the missing information.

topics.title: uncertainty
topics.explanation: Uncertainty can come from missing facts, contradictory sources or imperfect predictions. Name the actual gap; an unvalidated confidence percentage does not resolve it.

topics.title: user expectations
topics.explanation: Tell users what the assistant can do and where its information comes from. A carrier estimate should not be presented as a guaranteed arrival time.

topics.title: correction
topics.explanation: Make mistaken inputs and outputs easy to correct. After an address correction, show the new address and recompute dependent decisions instead of preserving the old plan.

topics.title: abstention
topics.explanation: Abstention means withholding an unsupported conclusion. The assistant can still explain the gap and provide a next step, such as requesting an order number.

topics.title: escalation
topics.explanation: Escalation transfers the case to someone with suitable evidence or authority. Include context and a clear handoff state; silently placing a case in a queue is not the same as having a human resolve it.

orientation: A delivery boundary defines which actions a system may take. A staged rollout exposes a change gradually, with an owner and a way to stop future use.
idea: Release the smallest useful capability whose failures you can observe and contain.
story: Meera’s team can buy a hosted assistant or build a routing component. A working demo settles neither choice. Both options need support, data access, operating costs and a way to switch when requirements change.

They start with draft replies for a small staff group. Humans still decide what to send. This boundary helps them inspect mistakes before expanding authority, while recording that stopping the feature cannot recall a message already sent.
example: A pilot creates 20 reply drafts and sends none automatically. Staff reject 4 drafts before customers see them. If automatic sending had been enabled on the same fictional outputs, 4 unsuitable replies would have reached customers. The model output is unchanged; the release boundary changes exposure.
trap: “We can roll back the code” does not mean every consequence can be reversed. Disabling future sends does not erase messages already delivered.

lab.question: How does the same set of 20 drafts affect customers under different delivery boundaries?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: these are assumed review decisions for invented drafts, not measured rollout safety or a real vendor comparison.

scenarios.label: 1 · Staff-only pilot
scenarios.result: The team can inspect failures without sending these drafts to customers.
scenarios.why: This tests draft usefulness, not the full customer workflow or the cost of sustained review.

scenarios.label: 2 · Approval gate
scenarios.result: Staff approval blocks four unsuitable drafts in this example.
scenarios.why: A human gate adds work and can itself fail. The zero here is a fixed fixture outcome, not a promise about reviewers.

scenarios.label: 3 · Auto-send
scenarios.result: Four unsuitable messages already reached customers.
scenarios.why: Stopping the feature contains future exposure; existing effects need a separate recovery plan.

mechanism: Compare build and buy against the same requirements: task quality, acceptable data handling, integration effort, total cost and who will operate the service. A vendor demo is only one input.
Define the release boundary in terms of permissions and users. “Draft for five trained staff” is more concrete than “small launch”, because it identifies what the system can actually do.
Choose a pilot gate and rollback owner before expansion. Monitor both output quality and the workflow; document how to disable future work and how to recover from actions already taken.

transfer.question: A hosted model becomes unavailable. Which preparation helps more: a favourite provider name or a tested fallback path?
transfer.answer: A tested fallback path. A stable application contract and retained input/output fixtures help evaluate another provider or return to manual work.

transfer.question: The draft-only pilot succeeds. Is automatic sending now proven safe?
transfer.answer: No. Automatic sending changes the authority boundary. Review-free operation needs its own evidence, monitoring and recovery design.

checks.question: What does a useful pilot boundary specify?
options: Users, allowed actions and stop conditions
checks.explanation: These details make the exposure and responsibility inspectable.

checks.question: What can code rollback usually not do by itself?
checks.explanation: External effects often require separate recovery even after software rollback.

checks.question: Which build-versus-buy claim is strongest?
options: Compare requirements, full costs and exit options
checks.explanation: Both choices carry integration and operating responsibilities; evaluate them for the actual workflow.

topics.title: build versus buy
topics.explanation: Building gives control but requires sustained engineering and operations. Buying can shorten integration work, but the team still owns customer outcomes and must evaluate the service against its requirements.

topics.title: feasibility
topics.explanation: Feasibility asks whether the necessary data, skills and operating conditions exist. A polished demo does not establish that daily latency, review capacity or quality targets can be met.

topics.title: vendor dependency
topics.explanation: Dependency grows when prompts, data formats and workflows assume one provider’s behaviour. Keep an explicit application contract and representative fixtures so replacement decisions can be tested rather than guessed.

topics.title: staged rollout
topics.explanation: A staged rollout expands exposure after predefined evidence gates. Draft-only, human-approved and automatic modes have different failure consequences, so passing one stage does not automatically justify the next.

orientation: A Python component is a reusable function or module with clear inputs and outputs. Reproducibility means another person can recreate its documented behaviour from the same code, environment and inputs.
idea: Make inputs, dependencies and failures visible instead of relying on notebook memory.
story: Meera normalizes ticket text in a notebook before routing it. One cell reads a global queue prefix left behind by an earlier experiment. The displayed result looks right, but restarting the notebook changes what happens.

She moves normalization into a function that receives both text and prefix. Now a colleague can see the whole contract. Type hints explain the expected values; explicit checks still need to reject invalid values at runtime.
example: With text “  Drill STOPPED  ” and prefix “urgent”, normalization produces “urgent:drill stopped”. Passing prefix “routine” intentionally changes the output. A hidden prefix makes this dependency easy to miss; a declared parameter makes it inspectable and testable in a clean process.
trap: A Python annotation such as text: str does not enforce the input type at runtime. Add validation where untrusted data enters, and preserve useful failure information.

lab.question: Can another developer explain this normalizer’s output without access to the old notebook session?
lab.limitation: Fixed synthetic case explorer: displayed outputs and failures are authored snapshots. This page does not execute Python or recreate an environment.

scenarios.label: 1 · Explicit inputs
scenarios.result: Both required fields are explicit valid strings.
scenarios.why: Given this fixture and function, the result can be reconstructed without notebook history.

scenarios.label: 2 · Hidden prefix
scenarios.result: The output depends on a value the caller cannot see.
scenarios.why: The text did not change; hidden configuration did. Pass the prefix explicitly and document its meaning.

scenarios.label: 3 · Hints alone
scenarios.result: The annotation does not reject 42 before the function runs.
scenarios.why: A boundary check could raise a clear TypeError instead of a later, less helpful method failure.

mechanism: Name each input and output, then isolate the transformation in a function. Keep environment access and network calls outside this small core where practical, so fixtures remain easy to reason about.
Validate external inputs deliberately and catch only failures you can handle. Returning an empty string for every exception hides whether a customer supplied bad data or the program is broken.
Record the Python version, dependency versions and configuration names with a clean reproduction command. Commit the code and fixtures, not secrets or the virtual environment directory.

transfer.question: Two developers use identical code but different dependency versions. Is identical behaviour established?
transfer.answer: No. Dependencies can change behaviour. Recreate the documented environment and compare the same fixtures before claiming reproduction.

transfer.question: Does locking dependencies guarantee identical results for every AI service?
transfer.answer: No. External APIs, hardware, random choices and changing data may also matter. State what the reproduction recipe controls and what it does not.

checks.question: Which change removes the hidden prefix dependency?
options: Pass prefix as a named input
Add a longer comment above the old cell
checks.explanation: A parameter exposes the dependency to callers and tests.

checks.question: What does text: str do by itself?
options: Describe the expected type for tools and readers
checks.explanation: Python does not enforce ordinary type annotations at runtime.

checks.question: Which item belongs in the repository?
options: A small fixture and reproduction instructions
checks.explanation: Commit the recipe and safe fixtures; recreate environments and supply secrets separately.

topics.title: Python types
topics.explanation: Types describe the kinds of values a function expects and returns. A static checker can flag misuse, but Python annotations alone do not validate an incoming JSON field.

topics.title: exceptions
topics.explanation: Exceptions report failures such as invalid input or unavailable files. Catch a specific failure when you have a recovery path; swallowing every exception can turn broken ticket processing into silent data loss.

topics.title: modules
topics.explanation: A module groups reusable Python definitions in a file. Move ticket normalization out of notebook execution order so another entry point can import it without repeating exploratory cells.

topics.title: environments
topics.explanation: A virtual environment isolates installed packages for a project. Recreate it from documented versions rather than checking its directory into Git; isolation alone does not pin dependencies.

topics.title: configuration
topics.explanation: Configuration holds choices that vary between runs, such as a queue prefix or endpoint. Make required values explicit and validate them at startup; secret values should not appear in committed fixtures or logs.

topics.title: Git
topics.explanation: Git records versions of tracked files so changes can be reviewed and compared. A commit identifies code, but untracked data, secrets and an undocumented runtime remain outside that reproducibility record.

orientation: NumPy stores numbers in arrays: ordered collections with a shape (the length of each axis) and a dtype (the stored value type). Here, one position means one rental. Start with M02-L01’s explicit input contract; now make the array shapes part of that contract.
idea: Match each rental’s days to its own daily rate, then verify the output shape and a hand-calculated cost before trusting the total.
story: Meera closes the equipment-rental desk with three SYNTHETIC bookings: a drill for 2 days at 12 fictional currency units per day, a sander for 4 days at 7, and a lamp for 3 days at 9. She wants one charge per booking. Think of two aligned ledger columns: day counts and daily rates. Multiplying across each row gives that rental’s cost.

She puts days [2, 4, 3] and rates [12, 7, 9] into separate one-dimensional NumPy arrays. Each has shape (3,), meaning one axis with three entries. The same position in each array must still identify the same rental; NumPy does not know the equipment names. A Python loop pairs the entries explicitly. Vectorization expresses the same work as days * rates, applying multiplication across the arrays.

Then Meera adds a column axis to days. Its shape becomes (3, 1), while rates stays (3,). NumPy accepts the multiplication, but now compares every day count with every rate. Each number resembles a reasonable rental charge. The ledger analogy stops here: NumPy aligns dimensions, not booking identities. Predict the number of outputs before choosing the cases below.
example: SYNTHETIC matched costs: drill 2 × 12 = 24; sander 4 × 7 = 28; lamp 3 × 9 = 27 fictional currency units. A loop and days * rates both return [24, 28, 27], shape (3,), with total 24 + 28 + 27 = 79. Rates are per day; multiplying by days gives the whole rental charge, not a daily rate.
trap: A successful operation can answer the wrong question. Shapes (3, 1) × (3,) produce (3, 3): nine pairwise costs instead of three matched costs. Even the first value, 24, is right. Check the entire first row and the output shape before summing; a plausible first cell is not enough.

lab.question: SYNTHETIC fixed fixtures: this page does not run NumPy in the browser. For Meera’s same three rentals, will each shape choice produce three matched costs, nine pairwise costs, or an error?
lab.limitation: SYNTHETIC fixed case explorer. Inputs, outputs and the failure shown here are authored fixtures, not browser-executed NumPy or production evidence. Bars count output entries on a shared 0–9 scale; zero after an error means no output, not a free rental. Run the separate data lab for executable evidence.

scenarios.label: 1 · SYNTHETIC matched rows
scenarios.result: Three matched costs; loop and vectorized total both equal 79 fictional currency units.
scenarios.why: Equal one-dimensional shapes pair the same positions. Check the sander: 4 days × 7 units/day = 28 units. This assumes both arrays preserve rental order.

scenarios.label: 2 · SYNTHETIC pairwise trap
scenarios.result: Nine plausible costs sum to 252 units, but Meera has only three bookings.
scenarios.why: Broadcasting aligns dimensions from the right; equal lengths or a length of 1 can expand. Here each day count meets all three rates. Row one is [24, 14, 18], not the drill’s single charge 24. Require matching one-dimensional inputs and rerun case 1; do not flatten the nine wrong charges.

scenarios.label: 3 · SYNTHETIC missing rate
evidence: ValueError; restore lamp rate 9, then rerun → total 79
scenarios.result: No costs are produced: the missing lamp rate makes the shapes incompatible.
scenarios.why: NumPy raises ValueError for these shapes; your calculator should reject them at its input boundary too. Do not truncate the loop or invent a zero rate. Recover the matched source rate and select case 1 to inspect the corrected result.

mechanism: Keep the meaning beside the shape. One axis of length three is (3,); three rows of one column is (3, 1). Broadcasting permits some unequal shapes, but our per-rental contract deliberately requires two equal one-dimensional arrays. Reject a column input even when NumPy could multiply it. Validate finite values before computing: NaN means not-a-number, and infinity is not a usable rate.

Compare the vectorized values with a loop and the hand calculation, not just with each other. Declare an absolute tolerance of 1e-9 fictional currency units and relative tolerance 0 for this tiny float64 fixture. A reduction combines values along an axis: costs.sum() turns [24, 28, 27] into 79. Reducing the wrong matrix just hides the extra combinations. Both implementations can agree while using incorrectly ordered rates.

Take away three habits: name each axis, reject shapes outside the business contract, and verify a row plus the output shape before reducing. Array means an ordered numeric collection; broadcasting aligns compatible dimensions; vectorization applies an operation across an array. In M02-L06, tables and join keys will help establish which rate belongs to which booking before we do this arithmetic.

transfer.question: A new SYNTHETIC booking sheet has days [5, 2] and matched rates [6, 11]. What output and shape should you expect? What if days is accidentally shaped (2, 1)?
transfer.answer: The matched output is [30, 22], shape (2,), total 52 units. A column-shaped day array multiplied by rates of shape (2,) gives [[30, 55], [12, 22]], shape (2, 2), total 119. Those extra cross-booking combinations are valid arithmetic but invalid billing.

transfer.question: Both arrays have shape (3,), and the loop agrees with vectorization. Does that prove the rates belong to the correct equipment?
transfer.answer: No. Shapes cannot check identity. With the same days [2, 4, 3] but reordered rates [7, 12, 9], both implementations return [14, 48, 27], total 89. Verify the booking-to-rate mapping and compare a known row. Neither agreement nor finite values alone establishes correct billing.

checks.question: Predict: days has shape (3, 1) and rates has shape (3,). What does days * rates produce?
checks.explanation: The trailing 1 expands across three rates, while the missing leading rate axis acts as length 1 and expands across three rentals. The result is (3, 3). Our billing contract should reject that input even though NumPy accepts it.

checks.question: A new SYNTHETIC rental fixture has days [1, 3] and rates [8, 5, 4]. What should a per-rental calculator do?
options: Use the first two rates and return [8, 15]
Reject the mismatch and recover the missing pairing
checks.explanation: Shapes (2,) and (3,) cannot broadcast. A zip-based loop would silently drop the third rate unless you check lengths first. Reject the mismatch; do not guess which rental or rate is missing.

checks.question: Meera sets trial = rates[:2], then trial[0] = 0. Why does the drill’s original rate change?
options: The basic slice is a view sharing the numeric storage
Every slice creates an independent copy
checks.explanation: Basic slicing returns a view. Assigning through trial changes rates too. Use rates[:2].copy() for an isolated experiment and test that the original stays unchanged; ordinary days * rates creates a separate result.

topics.title: NumPy arrays and dtypes
topics.explanation: A numeric ndarray has a shape and a common storage dtype. Use np.array([2, 4, 3], dtype=np.int64) for these whole-day counts and np.array([12, 7, 9], dtype=np.float64) for rates. A dtype describes representation, not units or validity. Fixed-width integers can overflow; floating-point amounts need declared comparison and rounding rules. Our small synthetic fixture is not a money-accounting policy.

topics.title: broadcasting
topics.explanation: Compare axis lengths from the right. Each pair must match or contain a 1; missing leading axes act as 1. Thus (3,) with (3,) gives three matched values, while (3, 1) with (3,) gives a 3 × 3 pairwise table. Lengths 3 and 2 cannot expand into one another. Broadcasting knows sizes, not rental identities.

topics.title: axis reductions
topics.explanation: An axis is a numbered dimension. A reduction such as sum combines values along the chosen dimension. For the pairwise table [[24, 14, 18], [48, 28, 36], [36, 21, 27]], sum(axis=1) removes the column axis and gives row totals [56, 112, 84]; sum(axis=0) removes the row axis and gives column totals [108, 63, 81]. Neither is the matched charge vector [24, 28, 27]. Omitting axis sums all nine entries to 252. Establish the intended shape before reducing.

topics.title: boolean indexing
topics.explanation: A boolean mask is an array of True/False selections. For matched costs [24, 28, 27], costs >= 27 is [False, True, True], so costs[costs >= 27] returns [28, 27]. Boolean indexing creates a copy when reading selected values; direct assignment such as costs[mask] = 0 still updates costs. Filtering expensive rentals is useful for inspection, but dropping invalid rates would misalign the billing inputs.

topics.title: views versus copies
topics.explanation: A view shares underlying storage; a copy has separate storage. With float64 rates [12, 7, 9], trial = rates[:2] followed by trial[0] = 0 changes rates to [0, 7, 9]. Start again and use trial = rates[:2].copy() before editing: rates remains [12, 7, 9]. Basic slices are views; advanced indexing reads are copies. Do not assume every reshape copies the data.

topics.title: vectorization
topics.explanation: Vectorization expresses repeated numeric work as array operations such as days * rates instead of a Python loop over bookings. It can reduce Python-level overhead, but this preview measures no speedup. A pairwise mistake can allocate n × n results rather than n. Keep a loop baseline, validate inputs before either path, and measure time and memory on a stated workload before making performance claims.

orientation: A service contract is an agreement about the requests a program accepts and the responses it returns. An API is the interface another program calls. Bring M02-L01’s habit of explicit inputs and tests to this boundary: receiving a reply and receiving usable data are different successes.
idea: Receiving a response and receiving valid business data are different successes.
story: Meera’s rental desk adds a ticket API for equipment bookings. A client, the program asking for work, sends a body containing the booking data and a header, a named piece of message metadata. The service, the program handling that request, must decide what the message means before accepting it. Her SYNTHETIC drill ticket has request_key "rent-001", equipment "drill", and days 2. The request key names the operation; it is not a password or proof that the booking was saved.

Think of a booking slip: first can Meera read it, then are its boxes filled correctly, then is it the form revision the desk supports? JSON is a text format for values; parsing turns that text into values the program can inspect. A lone { cannot be parsed. A complete ticket with days "2" can be parsed, but the quoted value is a string, not the positive integer her contract requires. Converting it silently would hide a client mistake.

Meera also requires X-Larnix-Version: 1. A well-formed ticket sent with version 2 still uses an unsupported contract. HTTP is the web’s request/response protocol; a form revision does not upgrade that protocol. A status code summarizes a response. Even a reply saying 200 can contain a broken ticket, so the client needs its own checks. The slip analogy stops at delivery: a missing network reply does not tell Meera whether a real server acted. Our local contract handler only validates and echoes a ticket; it opens no connection and saves no booking.
example: SYNTHETIC request/response trace, using the lab’s exact contract. With X-Larnix-Version: 1, body { → 400, body {"error":"malformed JSON"}. Body {"request_key":"rent-001","equipment":"drill","days":"2"} → 422, body {"error":"days must be a positive integer"}. Body {"request_key":"rent-001","equipment":"drill","days":2} → 200, body {"accepted":true,"ticket":{"request_key":"rent-001","equipment":"drill","days":2}}. Keep that valid body but send X-Larnix-Version: 2, or omit the header → 400, body {"error":"unsupported contract version; expected 1"}. Every lab response carries X-Larnix-Version: 1. If a faulty responder sends 200 with accepted=true but ticket.days="2", the client raises ContractError: invalid 200 ticket: days must be a positive integer. JSON spacing and object-key order do not change these values.
trap: A success status is not a validation function. In this fixture, the good request passes three checks: parse JSON, validate fields, check version. The good response must then pass the client’s checks too. A 200 means this handler accepted the contract; it does not mean a database row was committed. No automatic retry, transport failure or database write is executed by the case explorer.

lab.question: SYNTHETIC fixed fixtures: no Python handler, HTTP request or TypeScript validation runs in the browser. For the same rental ticket, predict which of three checks passes: JSON parsing, field validation, version compatibility.
lab.limitation: SYNTHETIC fixed case explorer. Responses are authored traces checked against the downloadable lab, not a running service or production evidence. Bars count passed and remaining checks on a shared 0–3 scale; remaining includes failed and unattempted checks. A validated ticket is not a saved booking.

scenarios.label: 1 · SYNTHETIC malformed JSON
scenarios.result: 400: malformed JSON. No field or version check is reached.
scenarios.why: One opening brace is not a complete document. Correct serialization before retrying; the same bytes still fail. This is an explicit rejection from the handler, not a connection failure.

scenarios.label: 2 · SYNTHETIC wrong field type
scenarios.result: 422: days must be a positive integer. JSON parsing succeeded; field validation did not.
scenarios.why: The value "2" has a different type from 2. The version check is not reached. Replace the string with the intended integer and select case 3; do not remove the validation rule.

scenarios.label: 3 · SYNTHETIC valid contract
scenarios.result: 200: the client accepts one validated ticket. This handler has not created a database record.
scenarios.why: Keep this body but use version 2 or omit the header: the result becomes 400 with unsupported contract version; expected 1 (2 / 3 checks pass). A fabricated 200 with ticket.days="2" also fails at the client. Validation applies on both sides of the boundary; inspect the worked trace and run the starter to reproduce these counterexamples.

mechanism: A boundary is where data enters code that must decide whether to trust its shape. A schema describes required fields and value types; validation actually checks them. Here the schema requires exactly request_key, equipment and days. The first two must be nonempty strings; days must be a positive integer, so even Python True is rejected despite being an int subclass. The handler stops at the first failed check: parsing, then fields, then version. A wrong-field ticket with a wrong version therefore reports the field error first.

The client receives status, headers and a body separately. It checks the response version, parses the body, rejects an error status, then checks the accepted/ticket envelope and ticket fields. An envelope is the outer object wrapping the result. TypeScript is a language that checks types during development; a type assertion such as value as Ticket makes a claim to its compiler without inspecting the received value. Runtime validation must establish the claim before application code relies on it.

Keep three habits: distinguish a missing reply from an explicit rejection; check both request and response values; choose recovery from the documented cause and operation. A retry repeats a request. Idempotency means repeating it has the same intended effect as doing it once, not that every reply is identical. The request_key needs a real server-side replay rule before it makes a create safe to repeat. The lab’s separate persistence part explores that rule. Next, M02-L03 asks how many valid requests the client should allow to run at once.

transfer.question: A second rental desk receives a 422 for days="3" and later a 503 after sending a corrected create request. Which is a candidate for retry, and what must be established before repeating the create?
transfer.answer: Correct the string duration before sending again; retrying that same 422 request cannot repair it. A 503 indicates service unavailability and can be a candidate for a bounded, delayed retry under the API’s policy, including Retry-After when supplied. It does not prove that no side effect occurred. Establish replay safety or look up the original request key first. A 5xx is not a blanket retry instruction, and some 4xx cases have their own recovery rules: the class alone is insufficient.

transfer.question: Another client sends {"request_key":"rent-009","equipment":"pump","days":3} with X-Larnix-Version: 2. Which response does this lab return? Would repeatedly sending version 2 or merely relabelling an incompatible payload as version 1 fix it?
transfer.answer: 400 with {"error":"unsupported contract version; expected 1"}. The fields pass, but the version gate fails. Use the supported contract only after checking the actual field meanings and representation; this particular body already matches version 1, so setting the header to 1 produces 200. A differently shaped version-2 payload would need conversion too. Omitting the header gives the same 400 reason. Repetition does not negotiate a version, and HTTP 426 is not an application-version response.

checks.question: Predict: Meera sends a complete ticket with days="2" and X-Larnix-Version: 1. Why does it receive 422?
options: It cannot be parsed as JSON
It violates the required field type
checks.explanation: The quoted value is a valid JSON string. This ticket contract requires a positive integer, so field validation returns 422 with days must be a positive integer. Use numeric 2 in the corrected request; neither another retry nor a type assertion changes the received value.

checks.question: A 200 reply contains ticket.days="2". What does a TypeScript assertion, value as Ticket, validate at runtime?
checks.explanation: The assertion adds no runtime check. The lab’s client validates the ticket and raises ContractError: invalid 200 ticket: days must be a positive integer. Keep external values unknown until checks establish their shape; a success status cannot replace those checks.

checks.question: In a real ticket-create service, the client times out before receiving a reply. What is the safe inference?
checks.explanation: Both failure before work and a lost reply after commit fit the observation. Investigate the original operation or use its documented replay mechanism before repeating a create. Our in-process contract handler performs no network request or persistence, so this is a transfer to a real service, not a timeout measured here.

topics.title: HTTP
topics.explanation: HTTP defines message semantics between clients and servers. A method names the requested action; status summarizes the response; headers carry metadata; the body holds content. For a real JSON endpoint, document method, path and content type as well as fields. Here handle(body, headers) models only the contract boundary in-process. It does not implement routing, Content-Type enforcement or a network transport. An error response supplies information a connection failure may not supply.

topics.title: JSON
topics.explanation: JSON text can encode objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null. In Meera’s ticket, days=2 and days="2" parse to different types. Parsing is not schema validation, and schema validation alone cannot prove equipment is available. The registered OpenAI structured-output guide makes the analogous distinction between valid JSON and schema adherence; its refusal and incomplete-output cases still need handling. This lesson makes no model calls and imports none of that guide’s examples.

topics.title: status codes
topics.explanation: RFC 9110 §15.5 covers client-error responses. This lab documents 400 for malformed JSON or an unsupported application-version header, with different error reasons; it uses 422 for readable JSON whose fields fail the contract. Its 200 response confirms validation only. It does not return 201 Created because this handler creates no resource. RFC 9110 §15.5.22 reserves 426 for a protocol upgrade and requires an Upgrade header: changing X-Larnix-Version is not that operation. Do not encode business meaning in status alone; inspect the documented error body.

topics.title: API versioning
topics.explanation: A contract version names the supported agreement about fields and their meaning. This handler requires X-Larnix-Version: 1 on valid requests and sends that header on every response, including errors. With otherwise valid fields, version 2 or no version produces 400 and unsupported contract version; expected 1. It checks fields before version, so tests must specify both inputs. Renaming days to hours or changing its unit requires a compatibility decision, not just changing a header string. The lab implements only version 1.

topics.title: TypeScript boundaries
topics.explanation: A declaration such as type Ticket = { request_key: string; equipment: string; days: number } describes values your code intends to use. Writing decoded as Ticket supplies no runtime evidence, and number alone does not require a positive integer. Treat decoded network input as unknown, then check the object, exact keys, nonempty strings and a positive integer before narrowing it. Check response version and accepted=true as well. The Python starter mirrors this discipline: TypedDict describes the client shape, while accept_response performs the actual validation.

steps: Download the runnable service lab or open labs/service-foundations/README.md. Follow its Python 3.12 test and report commands; no package installation is needed. Preserve the lab files. This SYNTHETIC contract exercise uses its first fixture, rent-001, and is not a benchmark or a live HTTP endpoint.

Save the starter as contract_probe.py in your own practice directory. Run python3 contract_probe.py --lab-dir /path/to/service-foundations. Record Python version and the fixture checksum from the lab report.

Extend your own client tests with a missing field, days=true, and a wrong response-version header. Write the corresponding TypeScript Ticket shape and a decoder from unknown that enforces the same rules; do not replace validation with as Ticket. For a real service design, document the method/path/content type and a bounded retry policy with replay safety. Explain separately what a 422, a version rejection and a timeout tell you. Network behavior and persistence are outside this starter.

# SYNTHETIC rental ticket; Python 3.12, standard library only.
# Save outside the read-only lab. Pass its directory via --lab-dir.
import argparse
import json
from pathlib import Path
import sys
from typing import TypedDict


class Ticket(TypedDict):
    request_key: str
    equipment: str
    days: int


def checked_ticket(lab, reply) -> Ticket:
    # TypedDict documents the shape; the next call checks actual values.
    return lab.accept_response(reply)


def probe(lab):
    ticket = {"request_key": "rent-001", "equipment": "drill", "days": 2}
    raw = json.dumps(ticket)
    cases = [
        ("malformed", "{", {"X-Larnix-Version": "1"}),
        ("wrong type", json.dumps({**ticket, "days": "2"}), {"X-Larnix-Version": "1"}),
        ("wrong version", raw, {"X-Larnix-Version": "2"}),
        ("missing version", raw, {}),
        ("valid", raw, {"X-Larnix-Version": "1"}),
    ]
    observed = []
    for label, body, headers in cases:
        reply = lab.handle(body, headers)
        try:
            value = checked_ticket(lab, reply)
            outcome = f"accepted {value['request_key']}"
        except lab.ContractError as error:
            outcome = str(error)
        row = (label, reply.status, json.loads(reply.body), outcome)
        observed.append(row)
        print(row)

    invalid = lab.response(200, {"accepted": True, "ticket": {**ticket, "days": "2"}})
    try:
        checked_ticket(lab, invalid)
    except lab.ContractError as error:
        print("invalid 200 rejected:", error)
    else:
        raise RuntimeError("client accepted invalid data")
    return observed


if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description="SYNTHETIC contract probe; no network")
    parser.add_argument("--lab-dir", required=True, type=Path)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    sys.path.insert(0, str(args.lab_dir.resolve()))
    import lab  # Your local, unchanged service-foundations/lab.py
    probe(lab)
# TODO: add missing-field, boolean-days and response-version tests.
# TODO: implement the same boundary checks in a TypeScript decoder from unknown.

orientation: A valid ticket can still wait too long or consume a slot after its customer leaves. Concurrency overlaps waiting work; bounded concurrency controls how much may enter a scarce resource at once.
idea: Bound admission and active calls separately, then await cleanup when work is cancelled.
story: Meera can now validate a rental ticket and reject an invalid reply. At opening time, five customers ask about equipment. The provider can handle two active checks. Calling it once for each customer, one after another, leaves capacity idle during waits; starting every check together ignores the two-slot limit. She needs somewhere for tickets to wait and a rule for admitting them.

Think of two telephone lines and a tray of request cards. A semaphore is the local slot counter: a caller acquires a slot before using a line and releases it on exit. A queue holds cards awaiting workers, the tasks that take and process them. A task is a scheduled coroutine, an async function’s resumable execution. A full tray must slow admission: this is backpressure, pressure from busy downstream work reaching its producer.

Unlike two human operators, Python’s event loop runs one task’s Python code at a time in its thread, switching when work suspends. The event loop is the scheduler for that cooperative progress. A customer leaving asks for cancellation; it does not instantly free a line. Meera waits for cleanup before reusing the slot. The five-ticket paper timeline explains that accounting. The downloadable SYNTHETIC lab uses four fixture tickets and records its own counters separately.
example: SYNTHETIC paper timeline, five tickets A–E and two slots; waiting means all arrived but not active tickets, not queue.qsize(). Each tuple is (active, waiting, cancelled, completed). Arrival: (0,5,0,0). Admit A and B: (2,3,0,0). Request cancellation of A: still (2,3,0,0), pending cleanup. After A exits: (1,3,1,0). Admit C: (2,2,1,0). B and C finish: (0,2,1,2). Admit D and E: (2,0,1,2). They finish: (0,0,1,4). Each row sums to five; these are chosen steps, not measured scheduling times. Separately, the four-ticket lab returns rent-001, rent-002, rent-003, rent-004 in input order with max_active=2, max_queued=2, active_after=0. Ordered results do not prove completion order.
trap: Two permits do not mean two allocated tasks. A million tasks waiting for the same semaphore still occupy memory. Bound the queue and worker population too. Even the lab retains its input list, result list and diagnostic events, so it is not a constant-memory client. Releasing a local slot proves local cleanup, not that a remote booking was stopped or undone.

lab.question: SYNTHETIC fixed fixtures: no Python event loop or provider runs in the browser. Predict the peak active count, compare it with capacity, then check the final active count. These three cases quote the downloadable lab’s four-ticket fixture and separate two-ticket cancellation probe, not the five-ticket paper timeline.
lab.limitation: SYNTHETIC in-process lab counters, shown as fixed cases. MockProvider.active counts entered calls until their finally cleanup; max_active records the peak. These counts are not elapsed times, throughput, fairness or evidence of remote cancellation. Timeout and streaming extensions are described separately; the lab itself returns whole tickets.

scenarios.label: 1 · SYNTHETIC bounded client
scenarios.result: All four tickets return; peak active calls equal capacity two and the final active count is zero.
scenarios.why: bounded_client uses Queue(maxsize=2), three fixed workers and Semaphore(2). A worker can hold a dequeued ticket while waiting for a permit; max_queued is not total waiting work. await queue.put slows the producer when the queue is full. The result list stores each ticket at its original index, so input order is preserved without promising completion order.

scenarios.label: 2 · SYNTHETIC unlimited tasks
scenarios.result: Four calls overlap: the observed peak exceeds capacity two, even though all calls later exit.
scenarios.why: This deliberately broken path bypasses the queue and semaphore. The mock accepts the calls; check_capacity rejects the recorded peak afterwards. It detects the violation rather than preventing overload or measuring a real provider’s rejection rate. A final count of zero cannot erase a peak of four.

scenarios.label: 3 · SYNTHETIC cancel + cleanup
scenarios.result: The cancelled first request releases the only slot; rent-002 enters and completes.
scenarios.why: The event gate keeps rent-001 active while rent-002 waits for the semaphore. Cancelling and awaiting the first task propagates CancelledError, runs the provider’s finally and exits async with semaphore. The follower then enters. This probe has capacity one, unlike the capacity-two bounded run. Neither local cancellation nor the final zero establishes a remote outcome.

mechanism: A pending await gives other work a chance to progress; it is not a promise that every await suspends. In the lab, the mock’s cooperative waits let calls overlap, and the instrumented entry/exit counter proves how many are inside. Queue(maxsize=2) bounds queued items; three fixed worker tasks avoid one task per ticket; Semaphore(2) bounds the provider section. The producer awaits space rather than dropping tickets. Inputs and results remain stored, so admission control here is narrower than a bound on all process memory.

Cancellation is a request, not an immediate kill. The cancelled task must reach a cancellation opportunity and unwind its cleanup. In limited_request, async with releases the permit; in MockProvider.request, finally decrements active. The cancellation probe awaits the cancelled task and then observes rent-002 enter. For a timeout example, put a gated request inside asyncio.timeout: when its deadline expires, local cancellation runs the same cleanup and the caller catches TimeoutError outside the context. Cleanup can delay return beyond the deadline; swallowing CancelledError would break the intended path.

Streaming means delivering pieces before the result is complete. In a separate SYNTHETIC extension, rent-001 first emits “Checking drill”, then waits for its ticket result. That one progress chunk is not a completed ticket. Cancel while the next chunk is pending: await the cancelled read, close the local stream and keep the result marked incomplete. A remote provider could already have acted; local closure gives no rollback guarantee. Remember the three boundaries: bound admission, bound active calls, and distinguish partial output from completion. M02-L04 next asks what a durable write proves after a response is lost.

transfer.question: Meera moves a blocking SDK call into async def. While it waits, the other rental tickets and their timeout callbacks stop progressing. Why, and what should she change?
transfer.answer: async def does not change the SDK’s blocking behavior. Its call occupies the event-loop thread instead of suspending. Use an asynchronous API, or move suitable blocking I/O to asyncio.to_thread and bound that work too. Cancelling the awaiting task does not forcibly stop an already running thread or undo a remote effect. A CPU-heavy Python loop needs a separate execution strategy; adding await around unrelated code is not a cure.

transfer.question: A new arrival stream creates one million tasks, each waiting behind Semaphore(2). Has Meera bounded memory, and would adding a queue after task creation fix it?
transfer.answer: No. The semaphore protects only two active entries; the waiting million tasks already exist. Feed a bounded queue from a producer that awaits space, and use a fixed worker population rather than a task per arrival. Decide whether a full queue should wait within a deadline or reject admission. Bound retained inputs, results and diagnostics as well; the four-ticket lab keeps those in memory and therefore makes no constant-memory claim.

checks.question: Predict: three workers share Semaphore(2). What does that semaphore directly bound?
options: Active entries to its protected section
checks.explanation: At most two active entries to the protected provider section in this client. In the bounded fixture, max_active=2 despite worker_tasks=3. Waiting tasks, stored inputs and calls from other processes are outside this semaphore’s scope.

checks.question: rent-001 is cancelled while rent-002 waits for the only slot. What should cleanup do?
options: Release resources and usually propagate cancellation
checks.explanation: Release resources and let CancelledError propagate so the caller can observe cancellation. The lab awaits rent-001’s exit, sees rent-002 enter and finish, and records max_active=1, active_after=0. Calling cancel() alone is not the cleanup evidence, and this does not prove a remote operation stopped.

checks.question: Meera uses async def but a blocking call freezes all other tickets. Why can async code still stall?
options: Blocking work can occupy the event-loop thread
All async code is automatically parallel
Every await creates a new process
checks.explanation: The event loop cannot advance other tasks while synchronous work occupies its thread. Concurrency relies on cooperative suspension; async def neither creates a separate process nor makes a blocking call asynchronous. Even deadline callbacks can be delayed by that blocking work.

topics.title: asyncio
topics.explanation: asyncio supplies the event loop and cooperative I/O tools. In Meera’s mock, await asyncio.sleep(0) deliberately yields without claiming a realistic latency. A pending Event.wait also suspends until signalled or cancelled. A blocking sleep or CPU-heavy loop inside async def prevents that cooperation. Use the provider counter to test overlap, not the mere presence of async syntax.

topics.title: tasks
topics.explanation: Calling an async function creates a coroutine object; scheduling it as a Task lets it progress with other work. Keep ownership of its lifetime and failures. The lab creates capacity + 1 workers in a TaskGroup, which awaits them and cancels siblings if a worker fails. Three workers can take tickets, but only two can hold provider permits. Indexed result storage preserves input order, not a promise about which task finishes first.

topics.title: timeouts
topics.explanation: A deadline bounds intended waiting, not guaranteed wall-clock completion. asyncio.timeout cancels the current task on expiry and converts its cancellation to TimeoutError outside the context; wait_for normally cancels its awaited operation and waits for cancellation to finish. The lab’s two-second wait_for calls are guards for expected test events, not provider service-level targets. The practice extension forces a deadline after an entry event, then checks active_after=0; no elapsed-time result is claimed.

topics.title: cancellation
topics.explanation: Task.cancel requests that CancelledError be raised at the next opportunity. The lab’s gate makes the cancellation point observable. After the provider’s finally decrements active, exiting async with semaphore releases its permit. Await the task to observe its outcome, normally propagate cancellation after cleanup, and do not report it as a successful ticket. The one-slot probe demonstrates local reuse by rent-002; remote reconciliation remains a separate concern.

topics.title: queues
topics.explanation: A Queue(maxsize=2) stores at most two queued items; await put waits for space. It does not count a ticket already taken by a worker waiting on a semaphore. task_done in a finally block balances each get, and join waits for that bookkeeping to reach zero; it is not itself a business-success check. The lab also enqueues one None stop marker per worker. Its max_queued samples ticket admission, not a complete history of every queue transition. The producer and fixed workers create backpressure, while retained inputs, results and diagnostic events still grow with the fixture.

topics.title: streaming
topics.explanation: A stream exposes pieces as they arrive; its protocol must say what makes a complete result. “Checking drill” is progress only. The practice extension uses an async generator, a local producer that yields pieces, and labels its ticket chunk complete. Cancelling a pending read unwinds the mock request; aclose closes this local generator. With real asyncio network streams, use the transport’s close and wait_closed lifecycle as appropriate. Closing locally cannot retract bytes already sent or prove a remote booking was cancelled. Buffer partial output separately, mark interruption explicitly, and require reconciliation before treating an uncertain remote effect as absent.

# SYNTHETIC companion: unchanged lab plus local timeout/stream extensions.
import argparse
import asyncio
import json
from pathlib import Path
import sys

async def stream_ticket(lab, provider, slots, ticket):
    yield {"kind": "partial", "text": "Checking drill"}
    result = await lab.limited_request(provider, slots, ticket)
    yield {"kind": "complete", "ticket": result}

async def extensions(lab, ticket):
    provider = lab.MockProvider(asyncio.Event())
    slots = asyncio.Semaphore(1)
    task = asyncio.create_task(lab.limited_request(provider, slots, ticket))
    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(provider.entered.get(), 2)
        # Expire on the next event-loop turn, after the request has entered.
        try:
            async with asyncio.timeout(-1):
                await task
        except TimeoutError:
            timeout = {"error": "TimeoutError", "active_after": provider.active}
        else:
            raise RuntimeError("expected timeout")
    finally:
        if not task.done():
            task.cancel()
        await asyncio.gather(task, return_exceptions=True)

    provider = lab.MockProvider(asyncio.Event())
    stream = stream_ticket(lab, provider, slots, ticket)
    chunks = [await anext(stream)]
    read = asyncio.create_task(anext(stream))
    try:
        await asyncio.wait_for(provider.entered.get(), 2)
        read.cancel()
        try:
            chunks.append(await read)
        except asyncio.CancelledError:
            pass  # The cancelled read is reported below, never as completion.
        else:
            raise RuntimeError("expected cancelled stream read")
    finally:
        if not read.done():
            read.cancel()
        await asyncio.gather(read, return_exceptions=True)
        await stream.aclose()
    interrupted = {"error": "CancelledError", "partial": len(chunks),
                   "completed": 0, "active_after": provider.active}
    complete = [chunk async for chunk in
                stream_ticket(lab, lab.MockProvider(), slots, ticket)]
    if [chunk["kind"] for chunk in complete] != ["partial", "complete"]:
        raise RuntimeError("unexpected stream protocol")
    return {"timeout": timeout, "interrupted_stream": interrupted,
            "normal_stream": {"partial": 1, "completed": 1}}

async def probe(lab):
    tickets = json.loads(lab.FIXTURE.read_text())
    result = {"lab": await lab.concurrency_cases(tickets),
              "extensions": await extensions(lab, tickets[0])}
    print(json.dumps(result, indent=2, sort_keys=True))
    return result

if __name__ == "__main__":
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--lab-dir", required=True, type=Path)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    sys.path.insert(0, str(args.lab_dir.resolve()))
    import lab
    asyncio.run(probe(lab))

orientation: Stopping a local task cannot tell you whether its database write committed. A transaction makes related writes all-or-nothing; a stable request key lets a later attempt recognize an earlier one.
idea: Commit related rows together, recognize repeated request keys, and test what remains after failure.
story: Meera’s rental desk can now validate tickets and release cancelled provider slots. It still needs a record the next worker can inspect. A row is one stored record; a table is a collection of rows with named columns. For request rent-001, the ticket row says drill, two days. Audit rows record the steps accepted, validated and recorded. One ticket therefore needs three audit rows in this SYNTHETIC fixture, not one row in total.

Her first design saves the ticket, then saves its audit trail separately. If the second part fails, the ticket survives without any audit rows. A transaction groups these related writes: commit accepts the group, while rollback discards its uncommitted changes. Atomic means the group takes effect as a whole. Meera wants either one ticket with all three events or none of this new request’s rows. A faster query cannot repair the wrong write boundary.

Now suppose commit succeeds, but its response is lost. The stored rows exist even though the customer sees no confirmation. Repeating the same request_key identifies the same intended operation; inventing a new key would look like a new booking. The lab uses an in-memory SQLite database to make these cases reproducible. It demonstrates local commit and rollback while that connection lives, not persistence through process exit or a disk crash. The PostgreSQL readings explain the production database concepts; they are not evidence that this lab ran PostgreSQL.
example: SYNTHETIC worked row ledger for rent-001 (drill, days=2). Read each pair as (ticket rows, audit rows): fresh store (0,0); separate ticket commit then failure before audit insert (1,0); a fresh store with the lab’s crash inside one transaction (0,0); retry and commit, then lose the response (1,3); replay the same key and payload (1,3), returning {'ticket_id': 1, 'replayed': True}; rejected direct duplicate (1,3); rejected changed-payload replay (1,3). The separate-write baseline is a companion counterexample, not a mode of store_ticket. The committed ticket has events accepted, validated, recorded: joining it to audit gives 1 × 3 = 3 rows, but only 1 distinct ticket. The companion prints this ledger as a stage/tickets/audits table.
trap: Rollback protects uncommitted database writes; it cannot undo an earlier separate commit, recover a lost response, or unsend an external email. A UNIQUE request key rejects duplicate inserts, but only the application’s replay policy decides whether an existing ticket is the same request. Three joined rows can still describe one ticket.

lab.question: SYNTHETIC fixed fixtures: no SQL or database runs in the browser. Predict which rows remain after each failure. The separate-write case is an explicitly broken companion baseline; the transaction and lost-response cases quote the read-only SQLite lab.
lab.limitation: SYNTHETIC local row counts, shown as fixed cases. The lab uses in-memory SQLite and injected Python exceptions, not a server crash or network outage. It does not show server failure modes, isolation levels beyond SQLite’s, connection pools or migration tooling. No disk durability, concurrent-client replay safety or PostgreSQL execution is demonstrated.

scenarios.label: 1 · SYNTHETIC separate writes
evidence: RuntimeError: separate-write failure before audit insert
First commit survives; second transaction has no audit rows
scenarios.result: The ticket remains without its required three-event audit trail.
scenarios.why: The companion uses the lab schema but deliberately commits the ticket independently, then raises before writing any audits. The second rollback cannot undo the first commit. This is a separate negative example; the lab’s store_ticket always groups the ticket and audits in one transaction.

scenarios.label: 2 · SYNTHETIC transaction crash
evidence: InjectedCrash: crash after ticket insert, before audit insert
scenarios.result: Neither the new ticket nor any audit row remains after the injected exception.
scenarios.why: Inside store_ticket, the ticket insert and all three audit inserts share with connection. The injected exception exits that context before the audit inserts and rolls the ticket back. This fresh-store result is zero/zero; rollback would preserve previously committed tickets. The exception is not a process kill or disk failure.

scenarios.label: 3 · SYNTHETIC lost response + replay
evidence: LostResponse: response lost after commit; outcome unknown to client
scenarios.result: One ticket and three audit rows survive; replay returns the existing ticket without another insert.
scenarios.why: ingest finds request_key rent-001, compares equipment and days, and returns ticket_id 1 with replayed=True. Direct store_ticket insertion of that key instead raises DuplicateRequest: duplicate request key: rent-001. Reusing it with days=9 raises DuplicateRequest: request key reused with different ticket: rent-001. Both rejections leave the existing one ticket and three audits intact. This single-client lookup-then-insert flow does not resolve concurrent replay races.

mechanism: Start with an invariant, a condition every accepted operation must preserve: this ticket creation commits one ticket and its three audit events together. SQL is the language used to query and change these tables. The lab’s store_ticket uses parameterized SQL, passing values separately from command text, inside one transaction. Its injected failure occurs after the ticket insert but before any audit insert. Rollback removes that uncommitted ticket. In the separate-write baseline, the ticket was already committed, so the same intended grouping is absent. Always inspect the tables after failure, not just the exception message.

A stable request key belongs to a logical operation, not to one network attempt. The schema declares request_key NOT NULL UNIQUE: it must exist and cannot repeat. ingest first looks it up and compares equipment and days; the same payload replays, a different payload conflicts. An index is a lookup structure; SQLite creates one for this UNIQUE constraint, supporting the request-key search as well as enforcing uniqueness. It does not make a read followed by an insert race-free across clients, or prove that the caller received the commit response.

A join pairs rows satisfying its match condition. Here audit.ticket_id matches tickets.id, so the three events repeat ticket 1 three times. COUNT(*) returns 3 joined rows; COUNT(DISTINCT tickets.id) returns 1 ticket represented in that join. The lab rejects treating 3 as the ticket count: JoinCardinalityError: joined rows are not ticket count: 3 != 1. Keep three checks separate: transaction tests for partial writes, replay tests for repeated requests, and join tests for the unit being counted. The next mathematical lessons build on the same habit of checking what a number represents.

transfer.question: A rental request committed, but the client received no reply. Should its retry use a new request key, and what if the duration changed?
transfer.answer: Keep the original key for the same intended operation and the same payload. In this fixture, replaying rent-001/drill/2 returns ticket_id 1 with replayed=True and leaves 1 ticket / 3 audits. Changing days to 9 under that key raises DuplicateRequest: request key reused with different ticket: rent-001; do not silently overwrite the first request. A deliberate new booking needs a new key. Across concurrent clients, lookup then insert can race: the uniqueness constraint prevents a second stored key, but the application still needs an explicit conflict/reconciliation policy.

transfer.question: One ticket has three audit events. A dashboard joins tickets to audit and reports COUNT(*)=3 as “bookings”. Is the store duplicated, and is COUNT(DISTINCT tickets.id) always the total of all tickets?
transfer.answer: No duplicate ticket follows from those three rows: one ticket joined to three events produces three pairs. In the lab, COUNT(DISTINCT tickets.id)=1 within that joined result. An inner join omits tickets with no matching audit, so even DISTINCT there is not automatically the count of all stored tickets. Count the tickets table for that question, or choose a left join deliberately and test a ticket with no audit. Fix the query’s meaning before treating a row-count difference as a storage bug.

checks.question: Predict: the new ticket insert succeeds, then an exception occurs before its audits. What preserves the ticket-plus-audit invariant?
checks.explanation: One transaction with rollback leaves 0 new tickets and 0 audits in the fresh lab store. Separate commits leave the first ticket behind. An index can locate or constrain a key, but it cannot group independent commits into one atomic change.

checks.question: The lab commits ticket 1 and its three audit rows, then loses the response. What can the client’s missing reply mean?
options: The data exists although the client is unsure
checks.explanation: The rows exist although the client is unsure: after_lost_response is 1 ticket / 3 audits. LostResponse is raised after commit. Retrying the same key and payload returns the existing ticket; rollback is not inferred from silence.

checks.question: What should a stable, unique request key enforce together with the application’s replay handling?
options: A fresh key on every retry
checks.explanation: One logical request has one documented identity. Same key and same payload reuse ticket 1; direct duplicate insertion and a conflicting payload are rejected explicitly. A new key on every retry would defeat recognition, and uniqueness alone does not implement the replay response.

topics.title: SQL joins
topics.explanation: The query joins tickets to audit ON tickets.id = audit.ticket_id. Its unit is a matching pair, so events accepted, validated and recorded yield three rows for ticket 1. The foreign key ensures each audit references a ticket when enabled; it does not require every ticket to have an audit. COUNT(*) counts pairs, while COUNT(DISTINCT tickets.id) counts ticket IDs present in the result. An inner join hides the separate-write baseline’s unaudited ticket. Use a left-join view or the tickets table when investigating missing audit trails; the PostgreSQL joins reading covers that distinction.

topics.title: transactions
topics.explanation: store_ticket groups the ticket insert and three audit inserts in with connection. The successful context commits; the injected exception rolls the current writes back. A previous committed record remains. A lost reply after commit belongs to a later boundary and cannot trigger an imaginary rollback. This in-memory SQLite connection disappears when closed: the lab tests atomic changes, not disk durability. PostgreSQL’s transaction reading describes database transaction concepts, but server failures, other isolation levels and external side effects need their own experiments.

topics.title: indexes
topics.explanation: ingest searches WHERE request_key = ?. An index provides a route to candidate rows without scanning the entire table for every such lookup; the planner still chooses a plan. In this schema SQLite creates a unique index for request_key TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE. The companion inspects PRAGMA index_list and index_info to identify it, rather than assuming an index name. Ordinary indexes do not prevent duplicate values; this unique constraint does. Indexes also cost storage and write maintenance. They do not make multiple writes atomic, confirm response delivery, or implement payload comparison and replay handling. No lookup-speed benchmark is claimed.

topics.title: tests
topics.explanation: A test executes a case and compares its result with an explicit expectation. Here a passing insert is insufficient: test a crash between writes, loss after commit, same-key replay, direct duplicate, changed-payload replay and the three-to-one join. Assert row counts as well as exact failure types, because an exception can occur after useful state was committed. The lesson fixture test imports the unchanged lab and compares these traces; the companion uses fresh stores and reports the broken baseline separately. Passing those cases does not exhaust all failure schedules.

topics.title: fixtures
topics.explanation: A fixture is controlled starting data and state for a repeatable test. This one uses rent-001, equipment drill, days 2 from fixtures/tickets.json. Start each independent comparison in a fresh in-memory store; within the lost-response/replay sequence keep the same connection, because existing state is the point. The three audit events deliberately expose join multiplication. Capture the actual Python/SQLite versions and fixture hash with the lab report. Production distributions, disk faults and concurrent-client races are absent from this invented workload.

topics.title: CI
topics.explanation: Continuous integration (CI) runs selected checks automatically for changes. Here make check validates curriculum/generated records, runs Node tests and JavaScript syntax checks, Python tests including the site build, and both runnable lab suites. The four hosted checks are “Schema, a11y & unit tests” (make check), “Notebook execution (R10)” (interactive engine tests plus execution of tracked notebooks if any exist), “Prose, spelling & links” (codespell, curriculum and rendered-link tests), and “preview” (build and upload the static artifact). A green run reports those checks in that environment, not a full accessibility audit, PostgreSQL migration test, production reliability proof or learner validation. The current repository has no authored notebooks; the check name does not claim otherwise.
